name: Cesare Beccaria
dossier: On Crimes and Punishments is quoted from James Anson Farrer's 1880 translation. Farrer's own chapters on Beccaria's life are not in the searched text.
voice: I ask whether the punishment is useful to the society that was offended.

entries.claim: Is death a penalty really useful and necessary for the security and good order of society?
entries.bears: Beccaria asks whether death is useful and necessary for the security and good order of society.

entries.claim: It is not the terrible yet brief sight of a criminal’s death, but the long and painful example of a man deprived of his liberty, who, having become as it were a beast of burthen, repays with his toil the society he has offended, which is the strongest restraint from crimes.
entries.bears: The lasting example of lost liberty and repaid toil is preferred to the brief sight of a death.

entries.claim: The very ages of ignorance, in which public morality inclines men to obey the dictates of private morality, serve as instruction and experience for the ages of enlightenment.
entries.bears: Ages of ignorance are said to bend public morality toward private morality, and to instruct later ages.

entries.claim: And the wonder will vanish altogether from the impartial student of human affairs, who will suspect that so great a moral machinery and so many restraints are perchance not needed, in order to render men happy and secure.
entries.loc: OF INJURIES AND OF HONOUR., paragraph 6
entries.bears: He suspects that so much moral machinery may not be required to make people happy and secure.

entries.claim: In the first case there will be a republic, formed of 20,000 little sovereignties; in the second the republican spirit will breathe, not only in the market-places and meetings of the people, but also within the domestic walls, wherein lies so great a part of human happiness or misery.
entries.bears: In the second case, the republican spirit is said to reach the household as well as the market.

entries.claim: He asks whether death is useful and necessary for the good order of society, and prefers the long example of a person who repays that society with toil.
entries.loc: On the mildness of punishments and on capital punishment
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. The test is usefulness to the society that was harmed.

entries.claim: Public morality in ignorant ages is said to lean on private morality, and he doubts that so much moral machinery is required for people to be happy and secure.
entries.loc: On the origin of punishments and on moral machinery
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. More restraints are not automatically more order.

entries.claim: A republican spirit, in the chapter on family spirit, is pictured not only in the market and the meeting of the people but also inside the house.
entries.bears: A summary, not a quotation. The household is part of the public spirit he describes.
